sources.entry: Snapcast - Synchronous multiroom audio server. GPL-3.0 C++/deb

summary.one_liner: Snapcast is a multiroom client-server audio system that streams time-synchronized audio from a server to clients, turning an existing audio player into a Sonos-like multiroom setup.
summary.what_it_does: Snapserver reads PCM audio from sources such as named pipes, ALSA capture devices, TCP, file, process stdout, PipeWire, JACK, librespot, and AirPlay, then encodes it (PCM, FLAC by default, Vorbis, or Opus) and sends it over TCP to Snapclients. Each client continuously synchronizes its clock with the server and plays chunks at the matching time through a system audio API, correcting drift by slightly speeding or slowing playback. Several sources can feed the server in parallel, and clients can be grouped to play the same stream. Control is available via a JSON-RPC API over TCP, HTTP(S), or WebSockets, covering volume, mute, renaming, stream assignment, and groups. The server ships with the Snapweb web app. The README says it is not a standalone player and is typically used with MPD or Mopidy.
use_cases: Multiroom music playback in several rooms
Extending MPD or Mopidy to multiple rooms
Routing line-in or ALSA audio to multiple speakers
Playing one audio source on many Linux, macOS, Windows or Android devices
how_to_run: sudo apt install snapserver snapclient (Debian packages; other distros listed in README)
brew install snapcast (macOS and Linux via Homebrew)
Configure sources in /etc/snapserver.conf under [stream], e.g. source = pipe:///tmp/snapfifo?name=Radio&sampleformat=48000:16:2&codec=flac
Point an audio player (e.g. MPD) at /tmp/snapfifo
Start snapclient with --player alsa (or another backend listed in README)
notable: Time-synchronized playback with drift correction by sample insertion or removal, typically under 0.2 ms deviation per the README
Multiple stream sources can run in parallel, and clients can be grouped into zones
Built-in Snapweb web app served by the server on port 1780 (HTTP) or 1788 (HTTPS)
Client packages and source builds for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Android, Windows, OpenWrt, and Raspberry Pi
Works as a backend for other players rather than as a standalone player
caveats: Not a standalone audio player; it needs an existing player (MPD, Mopidy, etc.) to feed audio
Client audio backends vary by OS, and some need specific device configuration
Roadmap items for adding or removing streams at runtime and a protocol specification remain unchecked
